Finding the leak

Part 2 of 3 · Choosing a franchise fairly, diagnosing it, and auditing the decisions it made

Faizan Khan

last-modified

Abstract

Data Premier League 2026, preliminary round, Task 1. The task has two problems inside it. Problem A: which franchise should a scouting report be about? Problem B: for that franchise, what is wrong, what did it do about it, and what should it do next? I answer A with a screen every team goes through, using three gates fixed in advance; only one team passes all three. I answer B with a separate set of hypotheses and a decision audit that follows the franchise season by season, from its 2023 data to the December 2023 auction to its 2024 results, and puts a number in runs, wins and crore on each step. Everything is in R and every number in the text is computed.

The short version.

Which team. I did not pick a franchise and then look for its problems. Every team went through the same three gates: did it win fewer games than its runs deserved in both seasons; does it have a weakness on the field that survives a multiple-testing correction, a ground adjustment and a second season; and did it pay more for its squad than its wins were worth. Only Royal Challengers Bengaluru passes all three.

What is wrong. Most of their reputation for bad bowling is their home ground. What is left, and what repeats in both seasons, is spin in the middle overs: -27.9 runs per 100 balls against the rest of the league, the worst cell of any team. It cost about 105 runs, or 1.2 wins, in 2023 and the same again in 2024.

What they did. After 2023 the data pointed at spin. At the December 2023 auction RCB released both of their main spinners, spent ₹36.2 crore of new money on pace and ₹2.0 crore on spin, and the middle-overs spin cell was no better in 2024 (-26.8 and then -29.0). Their 2024 turnaround, from 1 win in 7 to 6 in 7, came from the powerplay, not from the weak cell.

What next. Buy one Indian middle-overs spinner whose rate is in the league’s top quarter, with a bid ceiling set from projected wins, and move middle overs to the bowlers who are already good at them. Don’t spend the big money on more pace or on “clutch”.

1 The task, and how I approached it

The brief asks for a scouting report on one franchise across two seasons: diagnose the problem and suggest strategies. Read closely, that is two problems, and they need different methods.

  • Problem A: which team? A choice among ten. It needs a fair screen, so that the team is the output of an analysis and not an input to it.
  • Problem B: that team’s problem. A diagnosis and a set of decisions. It needs its own hypotheses, its own tests and a way to put a value on each decision.

I worked through both using the same six steps: describe the situation, search what others have already learned, name the obvious gap, choose a representation that ties the pieces together, write down hypotheses before testing them, and arrive at the key question. I borrowed this sequence from a problem-solving course, because it forces the order that analysis usually skips: you are not allowed to pick the answer first.

fig_six_steps(tibble(
  step = c("Situation", "Search", "Obvious gap", "Representation", "Hypotheses", "Key question"),
  text = c("Ten franchises, two seasons, ball-by-ball data and two auction sheets",
           "Mentor sessions and published work on run value, WAR, pressure and auctions",
           "Some teams win fewer games than their cricket deserves; why, and what did they do?",
           "A chain from money to squad to phases to runs to wins, and back to the next auction",
           "S1-S4 for choosing the team; H1-H8 for that team's problem and decisions",
           "Where is the leak, did the franchise fix it, and what is the cheapest fix now?")))

The six steps, as applied to this task.

1.1 Situation

A franchise cannot change the last two seasons. It can change three things: who bowls and bats when (deployment), who is in the squad (retention, trades and the auction) and what it pays (price discipline). An analysis that does not end in one of those three is description, not decision support. Amol Desai put it more simply in the mentor session: start at the decision, name the kind of question you are asking, and only then pick a model.

tribble(
  ~Question, ~Kind, ~`What it needs`,
  "Which franchise under-achieved relative to its own cricket, and has a fixable cause?", "Describe", "Outcome against an expectation of outcome; a fair screen",
  "What does a ball, a wicket, a player-season contribute?", "Estimate", "A state-dependent baseline to measure against",
  "How likely is the batting side to win from here?", "Predict", "A probability model that holds up out of sample",
  "Why did this team under-achieve?", "Explain", "Ground, game state and opposition held fixed",
  "Did the franchise's decisions address the problem?", "Audit", "What was known at the time, then what happened",
  "What should the franchise do next?", "Select", "Options priced in wins and crore, with uncertainty"
) |> tab(caption = "The kinds of question in this project")

1.2 Search: what is already known

Starting from zero would waste what others have worked out. These are the sources the method leans on, and what I take from each. The mentor sessions shaped the questions; the published work shaped the tools.

search_table() |>
  rename(Area = area, Source = source, `What I take from it` = what_we_take) |>
  tab(caption = "Prior work and what this project borrows from it")
Prior work and what this project borrows from it
Area Source What I take from it
Problem framing Amol Desai (DPL mentor session) Start at the decision, not the dataset. Name the kind of question (describe, estimate, predict, explain) before choosing a model. Watch for small samples, confounding, no overlap, survivorship and leakage.
Game state Himanish Ganjoo, T20 Basics (2026) Runs are worth different amounts at different moments; balls and wickets are the two resources. Expected runs depend on balls left, wickets down and the target. Leverage is p(six) minus p(wicket).
Runs above expected Bandyopadhyay, Runs Above Expected (arXiv 2608.18020) A multiplicative expectation fitted by Poisson backfitting with empirical-Bayes shrinkage, so phase and ground difficulty sit inside the baseline.
Replacement level and WAR Rafique, cricWAR (CMSAC 2022) Run value to runs above average to wins above replacement, with replacement set by workload and runs per win taken from the standings.
Set batters Kartikeya Date, A Cricketing View Balls already faced belongs in the expectation: a batter on 0 off 0 and on 30 off 20 are different propositions.
Roles and entry points Omkar Walunj (DPL mentor session) A batting position is a number on a team sheet; the entry point is the situation the batter walks into. Shrink a player towards his own role, not the league.
Auction value Malhotra, Journal of Sports Analytics 8(3), 2022 Hedonic price model on past performance; surplus is the benchmark price minus the price paid.
Price per workload Dan Weston, IPL auctions: market dynamics Lakh per ball involved as a blunt but honest efficiency number.
Pressure and variance Sahen Gupta (DPL mentor session) Variation under pressure is information, not noise. A jump in a player’s coefficient of variation across pressure states is a signal to act on.
Which numbers are stable Tom Nielsen, Cricket Sims Split-half stability by sample size: dot-ball rate settles fastest, wicket-based measures slowest.
Multiple comparisons Benjamini and Hochberg (1995); an earlier all-teams engine for this task Scanning many cells guarantees an extreme one; adjust for it and demand replication before acting.

1.3 The obvious gap

Part 1 showed that grounds, seasons and phases all move raw numbers a lot, and that most team weak spots move between seasons. The obvious gap is therefore not “which team was worst” (the table already says that) but which team under-achieved relative to its own cricket, in a way that repeats and that a franchise could act on. That is a narrower and more useful question, and it is the one Problem A answers.

1.4 Representation: the problem map

fig_problem_map()

The problem map for Task 1. Every analysis in this report measures one of these links.

The map is how I hold the whole task in my head. Money (purse and market) buys a squad. The squad is deployed into three phases, under conditions set by the ground. Phases produce runs for and against. Runs turn into wins, through how well a team converts close games. And wins, set against what the squad cost, give value per crore, which feeds back into the next auction. A franchise can only pull the levers on the left (purse, market, squad, deployment). Everything on the right is an outcome. So a useful diagnosis has to trace an outcome on the right back to a lever on the left.

Each link has a measurement attached: the hedonic price model for the market, runs above expected for the phases, the Pythagorean link from runs to wins, win probability for conversion, and WAR for value. Section 3 builds those tools, one after another, each one feeding the next.

1.5 Hypotheses for choosing the team

Written down before the screen was run, each with what would kill it:

selection_hypotheses() |>
  rename(ID = id, Hypothesis = hypothesis, Test = test, `Would falsify it` = falsifier) |>
  tab(caption = "Hypotheses for Problem A, recorded before testing")
Hypotheses for Problem A, recorded before testing
ID Hypothesis Test Would falsify it
S1 Some teams lose more games than their runs deserve, and not just in one season. Pythagorean gap per team-season; bootstrap share of resamples below expectation in both seasons. No team is below expectation in both seasons, or the gaps vanish under resampling.
S2 For at least one such team, the shortfall has a cause that can be located on the field. Phase x discipline x pace/spin cells on runs above average, three hurdles each. No cell clears all three hurdles for any team below expectation.
S3 The same team also got poor value for its money, so the problem reaches the front office. Surplus = WAR valued at the league rate minus spend, summed over the two seasons. The team’s spend is in line with or below what its WAR was worth.
S4 Money spent does not explain results at team level, so a team-level budget view is not enough. Correlation of squad spend with net run rate across 20 team-seasons. Spend explains a large share of net run rate.

1.6 The key questions

Problem A. Which franchise lost more games than its cricket deserved, in both seasons, with a cause on the field that survives scrutiny and a money problem that reaches the front office?

Problem B. For that franchise: which part of its cricket was persistently below what an average side would have produced in the same situations; did its auction decisions address that; and what is the cheapest change that would recover it now?

2 Problem A: choosing the team

2.1 Why one dimension is not enough

There are two easy ways to choose a team, and I tried both in earlier versions of this project.

The first is a single composite score: standardise a few measures and add them up. It works, but it hides why a team came top, and the weights are a matter of taste. My first version averaged a results residual with a money residual and put Punjab top; the money link turned out to have almost no fit, so I was averaging a real signal with noise.

The second is to scan one dimension in depth. An all-teams engine I built earlier for this task scanned every phase × discipline × pace/spin cell for every team and put each team’s worst cell through three hurdles. It was rigorous and it said “no single dominant defect” for half the league, which is what a method that is not manufacturing stories should say. But it found two teams with a “structural” defect and had nothing to say about results or money.

So this screen keeps the depth of the cell scan and adds the two things it lacked. Every team is described on every dimension, and the choice runs through three gates, each of which has to be passed on its own. Nothing is added up.

2.2 Gate 1: results against what the runs deserved

Given the runs a team scored and conceded, how many games should it have won? The Pythagorean model answers that: expected win share is \(R^k / (R^k + A^k)\), with the exponent fitted on all twenty team-seasons rather than borrowed from baseball.

fig_pythag(SCR)

Actual win percentage against Pythagorean expectation for every team-season.

The fitted exponent is k = 7.92, and expectation explains 54% of the variation in win percentage (mean absolute error 7.4 points). That is enough fit for the gap between actual and expected to mean something.

2 teams were below expectation in both seasons: RCB and PBKS. RCB won 5.4 percentage points fewer games than expected in 2023 and 10.9 fewer in 2024, about 2.4 wins short over the two seasons. They outscored their opponents overall and still won fewer than half their games.

fig_g1_boot(SCR)

How often each team stays below expectation in both seasons when its matches are resampled.

I want to be straight about how firm this is. Resampling each team’s matches 1,000 times, RCB stay below expectation in both seasons only 58% of the time. Part of any team’s conversion gap is luck in close games (Section 4 measures how much of RCB’s is). So Gate 1 identifies teams worth a closer look. It does not, by itself, prove a skill problem. That is what Gate 2 is for.

2.3 Gate 2: a cause on the field that survives scrutiny

For each team, the screen splits the game into 12 cells (batting and bowling × powerplay, middle, death × pace and spin) and measures each one in runs above average per 100 balls, from the team’s point of view, against the other nine teams. That measure comes from the expected-runs model in Section 3: every ball is compared with what an average player would have produced at that ground, in that over, with those wickets down, against that type of bowling. So a cell’s number already has the ground and the match situation taken out.

A team’s worst cell then has to clear three hurdles, each guarding against a different way of fooling yourself:

Hurdle Question Guards against
Multiplicity Still notable after a Benjamini-Hochberg correction across the team’s 12 cells (q < 0.10)? Picking the most extreme of many noisy numbers
Ground Still worse in a regression on raw runs with ground and season fixed effects and match-clustered errors (p < 0.05)? A home-ground artefact
Replication Worse in 2023 and in 2024, separately? One bad season 
fig_cell_scan(SCR)

Every team, every cell. Numbers are runs above the rest of the league per 100 balls; stars count hurdles cleared. 

fig_tiers(SCR)

Each team’s most defensible weakness and how many hurdles it clears.

Out of 83 team-cells with enough balls to judge, one clears all three hurdles: RCB’s middle-overs spin bowling, at -27.9 runs per 100 balls (95% interval -48.5 to -5.7). It has a Benjamini-Hochberg q of 0.061, keeps -23.0 per 100 balls with ground fixed effects (p = 0.001), and is -26.8 in 2023 and -29.0 in 2024. 4 teams have a cell that clears two hurdles, and 5 have nothing that clears more than one.

This agrees with the old all-teams engine, which used raw economy rather than runs above average and also put RCB’s middle-overs spin at the top of its list. Two independently built methods landing on the same cell is reassuring.

One sensitivity check, because thresholds are choices. RCB’s q is 0.061. At a stricter 5% false-discovery rate no team would clear Gate 2, and the screen would fall back to the team passing the most gates with the strongest cell, which is still RCB. The choice is not sitting on a knife edge.

2.4 Gate 3: money

From the value model in Section 3, every player-season has a WAR (wins above replacement), and the league has a going rate for a win: what all franchises together paid above the minimum, divided by the wins they got for it. A team’s surplus is the market value of its wins minus what it paid.

fig_money_gate(SCR, V)

Squad spend on players who played against squad WAR, with the league’s crore-per-WAR rate drawn as lines.

5 teams had a negative surplus over the two seasons. RCB’s was −₹11.7 crore, the most negative in the league, driven by 2023, when they paid ₹8.81 crore per win against a league rate of ₹6.15.

fig_spend_link(SCR)

Squad spend against net run rate, 20 team-seasons.

Hypothesis S4 holds: at team level, what a squad cost explains little about how it played (r = 0.36, p = 0.12). Squad WAR, built ball by ball without ever looking at a result, tracks win percentage far better (r = 0.70). If money buys anything, it does not show up in team totals, so the money question has to be asked at player level, which is what the decision audit in Section 5 does.

2.5 Every team on every dimension

The user of a scouting report will reasonably ask: “fine, but how does this team compare on everything else?” This is the full comparison, both seasons pooled.

fig_scorecard(SCR)

The full scorecard. Values are printed; colour is the team’s rank among the ten (green is best).

Read down the RCB column and the picture is specific rather than general. With the ground and match situation held fixed, their powerplay bowling ranks 1 of 10 and their death bowling 1. Their powerplay batting ranks 2. Their middle-overs bowling ranks 10 and their spin bowling 10. On money they rank 10 on surplus, and they won 0 of 3 close finishes. This is not a bad team. It is a good team with one hole, in exactly the phase that Part 1 found most closely tied to winning.

The three gates for every team.

Royal Challengers Bengaluru is the only team that passes all three gates, so it is the subject of the rest of this report. It is worth saying why the obvious alternatives are not:

  • Punjab passes Gates 1 and 3: they also under-converted in both seasons and also overpaid. But no cell of theirs clears more than one hurdle. Their problems were spread out, which makes them harder to diagnose and harder to fix with one decision.
  • Mumbai had the worst single season against expectation (2024), and their middle-overs spin also clears two hurdles. But they over-achieved in 2023, so the results gap does not repeat, and their surplus is positive.
  • Delhi, Gujarat and Lucknow have two-hurdle cells but won as many or more games than their runs deserved.

Verdicts on the selection hypotheses. S1 supported (two teams below expectation in both seasons, though neither firmly under resampling). S2 supported for RCB only. S3 supported for RCB (and for four others). S4 supported: spend does not explain results at team level.

3 The measuring tools

Testing the team’s problem properly needs three things the raw data do not give directly: an expectation for every ball, so a ball at Chinnaswamy in the 18th over is compared with balls like it; a win probability for every ball, so that “pressure” can be defined from the match state; and a value scale that puts batting, bowling and price on one axis. Each gets a ladder of models, from the simplest thing that could work to the most flexible thing I could defend, trained on 2023 and scored on 2024. A random split would let a model see half of a match whose other half is in the test set; worse, it answers the wrong question. Not “can this interpolate?” but “would it have been any use last April?”

Each tool feeds the next, along the problem map: expected runs give runs above expected; win probability turns runs and wickets into one currency; that gives runs per win; runs per win gives WAR; WAR and prices give value per crore. The detail is in Part 3; here is what each step found.

3.1 Ladder 1: expected runs per ball

Model What it is Why it is on the ladder
M0 The global mean The null
M1 Cell means by over and wickets Classic run expectancy, as in cricWAR
M2 Multiplicative log-linear model, Poisson backfitting, empirical-Bayes shrinkage on each factor Bandyopadhyay’s runs-above-expected structure; every factor is a readable multiplier
M3 Hierarchical Poisson model with batter, bowler and venue effects Partial pooling on people and places
M4 Gradient-boosted trees Non-linearity without being told where 
fig_exp_ladder(els)

Expected-runs ladder, scored on 2024 deliveries.

Boosting is the most accurate (2.7% better than the null on Poisson deviance); M2 is 2.1% better and is the only model whose calibration slope is essentially one (1.004). Nobody explains much of a single ball; cricket deliveries are mostly noise. For a measurement model, where the residual is the product, calibration matters more than the last half-percent of accuracy, so M2 is used everywhere downstream. Its venue factors also give a clean read on the grounds:

fig_venue_gamma(EL$m2_gammas$venue, HOME)

Venue run multipliers from M2, shrunk towards 1.

3.2 Ladder 2: win probability, WPA and leverage

fig_wp_ladder(WP$scores)

Out-of-sample log-loss for the win-probability ladder (lower is better).

The best model is W1, the one with the fewest fitted numbers: a three-parameter resource curve for expected remaining runs, fed through a Pythagorean link with the exponent fixed at 6, as in Himanish Ganjoo’s T20 Basics. The logistic and GAM models with many more parameters were worse on 2024. A parameter pinned by prior knowledge travelled better than the same parameter learned from one season. That is Amol Desai’s point about complexity being a cost, seen in the numbers.

W1 gives win probability added (WPA) for every ball and leverage, Ganjoo’s p(six) − p(wicket): how much the next ball could swing the match, known before it is bowled. Leverage is what defines “pressure” in Section 4, without looking at outcomes.

3.3 Ladder 3: runs to wins to crore

Runs above average per ball (runs above expected plus a wicket term, centred within season) roll up into WAR through a replacement level and a runs-per-win rate, following Rafique’s cricWAR. Runs per win comes from differentiating the Pythagorean model at parity: 4 × runs per match / k = 90.3 (cricWAR’s published IPL figure is 84.5). Squad WAR, built without looking at a result, correlates with wins at r = 0.75.

fig_team_war(V$team, TS, TEAM)

Squad WAR against wins, 20 team-seasons.

The league paid ₹6.15 crore per WAR in 2023 and ₹5.93 in 2024. By role and origin, Indian bowlers were the cheapest source of wins and overseas players the dearest:

fig_cr_per_war(V$money)

Crore paid per win above replacement, by role and origin.

3.4 Ladder 4: what the auction pays for

A hedonic price model in the style of Malhotra (2022) says overseas players cost about 170% more than Indian players in the same role and bowlers about 42% less than batters. Once last season’s WAR is in the model the market does pay for performance, but price explains only part of value. Combined with the chart above, the cheapest wins in this market are Indian bowlers.

fig_hedonic(V$hedonic)

Hedonic price models: coefficients on the log-price scale.

3.5 The pressure layer

Sahen Gupta’s PACE framework (pressure context, arousal signature, consistency, event sequence) shapes this part, along with his warning to compare a player with himself. The headline result is short: clutch is not repeatable in this data. A batter’s pressure differential in 2023 correlates with his 2024 figure at r = -0.28 (n = 18). The full layer is in Part 3.

4 Problem B, part 1: what is wrong with RCB?

4.1 A separate set of hypotheses

Problem A asked “which team?”. Problem B asks a different question, so it gets its own register, again written before the tests:

team_hypotheses(TA) |>
  rename(ID = id, Area = group, Hypothesis = hypothesis, `Would support it` = supports, `Would falsify it` = falsifies) |>
  tab(caption = sprintf("Hypotheses for %s, recorded before testing", TA))
Hypotheses for RCB, recorded before testing
ID Area Hypothesis Would support it Would falsify it
H1 Where RCB’s shortfall sits in one phase-and-discipline cell rather than being spread across the innings. One cell is an outlier against the league with ground and game state held fixed, in both seasons. No cell survives the multiple-testing adjustment, or the worst cell changes between seasons.
H2 Why It is a deployment problem: a better option in the squad is under-used in that cell. Inside the cell, a player with a clearly better rate has a small share of the balls. The most-used player in the cell is also the best available.
H3 Why It is a squad-building problem: nobody in the squad does that job well. No squad member with a real workload in the cell is above the league median for it. A good option exists in the squad, which makes it a deployment or form problem.
H4 Why What looks like a team weakness is really the home ground. The gap disappears once ground is held fixed, with match-clustered errors. The gap survives ground fixed effects at much the same size.
H5 Money The squad’s money sits on the roles that contribute least. Negative surplus is concentrated in one expensive group while a cheaper group carries the value. Price and contribution line up within what the sample can resolve.
H6 Pressure In tight games the problem is variability, not average level. The team’s record in close finishes is much worse than in other games, or key players’ variation jumps under pressure. Close-game record is in line with the rest, and variation is flat across pressure.
H7 Decisions The December 2023 auction did not address what 2023 had shown. New money went mainly to roles other than the weak cell, and the cell was no better in 2024. The new money went to the weak cell, or the cell improved in 2024.
H8 Decisions The 2024 turnaround came from somewhere other than the weak cell. Between the first and second halves of 2024, other phases improved much more than the weak cell. The weak cell is where most of the improvement happened.

H1 to H6 are about the cricket. H7 and H8 are about the franchise’s decisions, and Section 5 tests them.

4.2 H4: is it the ground?

On raw numbers RCB bowled badly: 9.57 an over conceded against 9.19 for everyone else. That is the familiar story. But Chinnaswamy is small, high and fast-scoring, and they bowl half their overs there.

fig_venue_check(vc)

Bowling gap to the league, raw and venue-adjusted, at home and away.

In a regression with match-clustered errors, the team’s overall bowling effect goes from +5.3 to -0.6 runs per 100 balls once ground fixed effects are added.

H4: supported for bowling overall. The general “can’t bowl” story is mostly the ground. That doesn’t make the problem go away; it relocates it. Whatever is left with the ground held fixed is the real target.

4.3 H1: is the shortfall concentrated?

fig_cells(X$cells_season, TEAM)

Runs above expected per 100 balls by phase and discipline, each season, with 95% match-bootstrap intervals. 

fig_mid_spin(VF, TEAM)

Middle-overs bowling by team and bowler type, both seasons.

With ground and situation held fixed, RCB’s batting is fine everywhere and their powerplay and death bowling rank 1 and 2 in the league. One phase stands out: middle-overs bowling, 10th of 10. Split by bowler type, it is almost entirely spin. RCB’s spinners in overs 7 to 15 were -24.1 runs per 100 balls against expectation, while every other team’s spinners averaged +3.8 (the gap of 27.9 is the cell value in the screen); the next-worst team was at -8.2. Their middle-overs pace, by contrast, went from -15.2 in 2023 to +5.0 in 2024, which is what a cell without a persistent problem looks like.

The spin split was chosen after seeing that the middle overs were the worst phase, which is how people find patterns in noise. The screen in Section 2 deals with that properly: middle-overs spin was one of 12 pre-defined cells for every team, the correction for multiplicity was applied across all 12, and it replicates out of sample. Treat 2023 as discovery (-22.9 per 100) and 2024 as the test (-25.3, p = 0.004): the squad changed and the number did not.

H1: supported. The shortfall sits in middle-overs spin, it is the worst cell in the league, it repeats in both seasons and it survives the ground adjustment. It cost about 105 runs in 2023 and 103 in 2024 against the rest of the league’s spinners: roughly 1.2 wins a season at 90 runs per win, or ₹7.0 crore at the league’s going rate.

4.4 H2 and H3: deployment or squad?

fig_squad_cell(X$squad_cell)

Every bowler with 24+ middle-overs balls for the team: share of the work against how good they are there (shrunk towards the average).

The most-used middle-overs bowler was Karn Sharma (17% of the balls), whose shrunk rate sits in the 2nd percentile of the league. The bowlers with a positive record there, Cameron Green, Mohammed Siraj and Glenn Maxwell, got 23% of the work. So there is a deployment problem. But none of them is a frontline spinner. Of the frontline spinners with a real share (Karn Sharma, Wanindu Hasaranga and Mayank Dagar), none is above the league’s median regular middle-overs spinner (shrunk +2.3 per 100). The best spin option was Glenn Maxwell, a part-timer whose main job is batting.

H2: partly supported. Better middle-overs options were under-used, but they are pace bowlers and part-timers and cannot carry the phase.

H3: supported. The squad had no spinner of even median quality for the middle overs. This is a missing archetype, not a good player having a bad year.

4.5 H5: was the money where it mattered?

fig_surplus(V$money, TEAM)

Realised surplus by player and season. Market value is WAR at the league’s going rate.

In 2023 RCB paid ₹8.81 crore per win above replacement against a league rate of ₹6.15, with a realised surplus of −₹19.7 crore. In 2024 they improved to ₹5.77 per win and a surplus of ₹8.1 crore, carried by cheap Indian players who over-delivered. The money lost sits mostly with expensive overseas players who either did not play much or did not perform.

H5: supported for 2023, weaker for 2024. Money sat on the roles with the market’s highest cost per win, while the archetype the squad lacked is in the cheapest part of the market.

4.6 H6: is it pressure, or is it luck?

fig_close(X$close, TEAM)

Win rate in close games against all other games, both seasons.

RCB played 3 close games over the two seasons (a chase still between 25% and 75% at the start of the 18th over) and won 0. In every other game they won 14 of 26. They lost only 2 of the 16 games in which they were at least 75% to win, about the league norm. So the results gap is not a habit of throwing away won games. A good part of it is a handful of coin-flips that landed the wrong way, plus a bowling cell that kept games closer than they needed to be. And clutch performance does not repeat from one season to the next (r = -0.28 for batters).

H6: rejected. No evidence that RCB’s players come apart under pressure in a way that would repeat. Paying for “clutch” would be paying for last year’s luck.

5 Problem B, part 2: what did the franchise do about it?

The diagnosis says what was wrong across two seasons. A franchise, though, did not get two seasons at once. It got 2023, then had to decide, then got 2024. So this section follows the decisions in the order they were made, and asks of each: what did the data say at the time, what did the franchise do, how did it turn out, and what would have been better.

Two rules. Anything labelled foresight uses only what was available at the time. Anything labelled hindsight uses later results and is there to grade a decision, not to pretend the franchise could have known. And nothing here is causal: a released player doing well elsewhere does not prove he would have done well at home.

fig_audit_timeline(A, SCR)

An analyst looking only at 2023 would have seen two clearly bad cells: middle-overs spin bowling (-26.8 per 100 balls) and batting against spin in the powerplay (-19.5, a small cell of 330 balls over two seasons). The bowling cell was the bigger and more expensive problem.

In 2023 the gap cost about 105 runs against an average spin attack, or 1.2 wins, worth about ₹7.2 crore at the going rate. RCB finished one win short of the play-offs that season.

RCB released both of their main spinners from 2023 (Shahbaz Ahmed and Wanindu Hasaranga, ₹13.2 crore of contracts). Releasing Wanindu Hasaranga was defensible on the numbers: he was the most expensive spinner and the worst of the regulars in the cell. But the replacements were Mayank Dagar and Swapnil Singh, for ₹2.0 crore between them, while ₹36.2 crore of new money went on pace: Alzarri Joseph, Cameron Green, Lockie Ferguson, Vijaykumar Vyshak, Yash Dayal. The largest single move, the trade for Cameron Green, was a pace-bowling allrounder.

On the record of 2023 alone, the auction went the other way from the diagnosis. The weakness was spin in the middle overs; 95% of the new bowling money went on pace.

Two readings of that table, and both matter.

Foresight. On 2023 evidence alone, the shrinkage model expects any one spinner to be only modestly better than RCB’s own (worth about 0.23 wins at best). A single season of middle-overs bowling does not separate spinners well; across these bowlers the 2023-to-2024 correlation is close to zero. The lesson for recruitment is to buy on several seasons of evidence, not one.

Hindsight. The spinners who did repeat were worth a lot. Axar Patel bowling RCB’s 2024 middle-overs spin balls at his own 2024 rate would have saved about 138 runs, or 1.5 wins (₹9.0 crore). Most of the established names would have been worth close to a full win.

None of those players was in the auction. The route to them was a trade, the same route RCB used for a ₹17.5 crore pace-bowling allrounder.

The 2024 season turned sharply: 1 win from 7, then 6 from 7. (This repeats the earlier RCB-only review, from this pipeline’s tables; the numbers agree closely, with small differences from how extras are counted.) H7: supported. The auction did not address what 2023 had shown: ₹36.2 crore of new money on pace, ₹2.0 crore on spin, and the cell was -26.8 and then -29.0.

H8: supported. The turnaround came from the powerplay (with bat and ball) and from the batting, not from the weak cell.

The cleanest way to put it: the franchise correctly spotted that its bowling needed work and spent heavily on it. The money bought a much better new-ball attack, and that was a big part of the 2024 recovery. But the specific, repeated, expensive hole in the middle overs was left as it was, two seasons running.

6 Problem B, part 3: what next

6.1 The options

The diagnosis points at one archetype, a middle-overs spinner who controls runs, and one deployment habit. The options follow the order in which a franchise can act: what is free, what costs money, and what to stop doing.

Two ways to count the prize. The measured cost of the problem is about 1.2 wins a season. That describes the past. What a franchise can expect to recover is smaller, because the players responsible would be expected to drift back towards average anyway. Projected on shrunk estimates, the current middle-overs spinners would run at about -2.6 per 100 balls next season. The decision is made on the smaller number.

fig_impact(RC$sims)

Simulated wins added per season for each option, on shrunk projections. 

sim |> arrange(desc(option)) |>
  transmute(Option = option, `Expected wins / season` = mean, `5th pct` = lo, `95th pct` = hi, `P(gain > 0)` = p_pos) |>
  tab(caption = sprintf("Projected effect per season. A spinner bowls three middle overs a match (%d balls a season); redeployment moves 120 balls.", O$spinner_balls), digits = 2)
Projected effect per season. A spinner bowls three middle overs a match (252 balls a season); redeployment moves 120 balls.
Option Expected wins / season 5th pct 95th pct P(gain > 0)
A. Redeploy only (free) 0.07 -0.09 0.22 0.76
B. Median regular spinner 0.14 -0.23 0.52 0.73
C. Top-quartile Indian spinner 0.24 -0.14 0.61 0.85
D. Elite spinner (best in league) 0.44 0.05 0.82 0.97

On shrunk projections a top-quartile Indian spinner is worth 0.24 wins a season with a 85% chance of being positive, and the best spinner in the league about 0.44. If the last two seasons’ gap simply repeated, the top-quartile spinner would be worth about 0.8 wins. These are modest numbers and I would rather say so. Two things make them matter: the margins (RCB missed the 2023 play-offs by one win and made 2024’s on net run rate), and the price (the archetype is in the cheapest part of the market).

6.2 Recommendation 1: redeploy now, for free

Give the middle overs to the bowlers who are good at them, within the four-over cap: more for Cameron Green, Mohammed Siraj and Glenn Maxwell, fewer for the spinners at the bottom of the league list in this phase. It is limited because those bowlers have other jobs, so it cannot be the whole answer.

The core that carried 2024 (Yash Dayal, Mohammed Siraj, Dinesh Karthik, Rajat Patidar and Faf du Plessis) came cheaply relative to what they produced. The two contracts that cost far more than they returned in 2024 were Glenn Maxwell and Alzarri Joseph. One season of WAR is noisy, so the two-season column sits next to it.

6.5 What not to do

  • Don’t buy “bowling” in general. Powerplay and death bowling were above average once the ground was accounted for, and the 2024 pace signings made the new ball even stronger. Another expensive overseas fast bowler addresses a problem that is mostly Chinnaswamy.
  • Don’t pay for clutch. It doesn’t repeat (r = -0.28 for batters, -0.24 for bowlers).
  • Don’t recruit spinners on one season. A single season of middle-overs bowling is a weak guide to the next.
  • Don’t judge bowlers on raw economy at home. Use venue-adjusted numbers in contract talks.

7 The decision

Decision. At the next auction, Royal Challengers Bengaluru should spend on one Indian specialist spinner whose shrunk middle-overs rate is in the league’s top quarter over more than one season, with a bid ceiling set from projected wins at the league’s going rate, and should move middle overs to its existing positive options from the next match. It should not spend its overseas slots or its largest bids on more pace bowling or on players sold as finishers.

What it is worth. About 0.3 wins a season on conservative, shrunk projections, and up to about 0.8 if the past two seasons’ gap persisted. In 2023 one more win was the difference between missing the play-offs and making them.

What would change my mind. If a third season showed middle-overs spin back near average with the same bowlers, the two-season pattern was noise and the money should go elsewhere. If ball-tracking showed the spin problem was specific to Chinnaswamy’s short square boundaries in a way the venue factor misses, the answer would shift towards a different type of spinner rather than a better one.

How to monitor it. Three numbers, every five matches: middle-overs spin runs above average per 100 balls (target: at least the league median); the share of middle-overs balls going to bowlers with positive shrunk rates (target: more than half); and cost per WAR against the league rate at season end.

ID Hypothesis Verdict Key evidence
H1 RCB’s shortfall sits in one phase-and-discipline cell rather than being spread across the innings. Supported Bowling: middle overs spin: -27.9 runs per 100 balls against the rest of the league (95% CI -48.5 to -5.7); BH q = 0.061; ground-adjusted -23.0 (p = 0.0014); -26.8 in 2023 and -29.0 in 2024.
H2 It is a deployment problem: a better option in the squad is under-used in that cell. Partly supported Best squad option with 60+ middle-overs balls (any bowling type): Cameron Green (+3.1 shrunk, 10% of balls). The most-used, Karn Sharma, was -5.9.
H3 It is a squad-building problem: nobody in the squad does that job well. Supported Frontline spinners with 60+ balls: Karn Sharma, Wanindu Hasaranga, Mayank Dagar. Shrunk rates -5.9, -6.5, -1.4; league median regular +2.3.
H4 What looks like a team weakness is really the home ground. Supported for bowling overall Bowling gap without ground terms +5.3 per 100, with ground fixed effects -0.6. The spin cell keeps -23.0 per 100 after ground fixed effects.
H5 The squad’s money sits on the roles that contribute least. Supported (2023), weaker (2024) Team surplus over two seasons -11.7 crore; 2023 crore per WAR 8.81 against a league rate of 6.15.
H6 In tight games the problem is variability, not average level. Rejected Close finishes: 0 won of 3; other games 14 of 26.
H7 The December 2023 auction did not address what 2023 had shown. Supported New money at the Dec 2023 auction: 36.2 crore on pace, 2.0 crore on spin. Middle-overs spin -26.8 per 100 in 2023, -29.0 in 2024.
H8 The 2024 turnaround came from somewhere other than the weak cell. Supported First vs second half of 2024: wins 1/7 to 6/7; powerplay bowling +43.2 per 100; middle-overs spin economy 10.12 to 9.06.

8 Epilogue: what actually happened next

The data stop in May 2024, and nothing below was used in the analysis. At the November 2024 mega auction Royal Challengers Bengaluru bought two spinners: Krunal Pandya for ₹5.75 crore and Suyash Sharma for ₹2.6 crore (Sportskeeda; Onmanorama). Krunal Pandya is 3rd on the shortlist above, and Suyash Sharma is on the 2023 list of regular middle-overs spinners. RCB won the 2025 title, beating Punjab by six runs in the final, and Krunal Pandya was player of the match with 2 for 17 from his four overs (cricket.com).

One outcome proves nothing on its own, and many things changed in a mega-auction year. But it is reassuring that the archetype this analysis points to, from two seasons of ball-by-ball data, is the one a real recruitment team went looking for a season later.

9 Limitations

  • Two seasons is not much. Player estimates are heavily shrunk, and the gate-1 result for every team is uncertain under resampling.
  • Auction prices are incomplete. Some replacement signings are not on the auction sheets and are left unpriced; trades are priced at the sheet value.
  • The audit is not causal. “Released player X did well elsewhere” mixes his skill with a new team, role and ground.
  • The foresight market is thin. Only a handful of auction-pool spinners had 2023 middle-overs evidence, so foresight comparisons rest on small samples.
  • WAR is a description, at a stated replacement level and runs-per-win rate. Other defensible choices would move the levels, not much the rankings.
